definition: But-for cause, sometimes used interchangeably with actual cause, is a necessary element for both liability in civil cases and a guilty verdict under much of criminal law.  In civil cases, but-for cause combines with proximate cause to fulfill the causation requirement of any tort.  In criminal cases, but-for cause is generally sufficient to establish causation, though some jurisdictions also allow proving causation through alternative theories.  See but-for test for more detailed information.  Similar to civil law, once actual cause is established, proximate cause must also be established to return a liable/guilty verdict.
